prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)
Description: The Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS) is sponsored by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. The MHS produces monthly regional estimates of the average sales price for new manufactured homes and more detailed annual estimates including selected characteristics of new manufactured homes. In addition, MHS produces monthly estimates of homes shipped by status. The statistics on shipments of new manufactured homes are produced by the Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS). They are rounded in the month of release and unrounded in subsequent months. Both not seasonally adjusted and seasonally adjusted annual rates of shipment estimates of new manufactured homes are released monthly.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)
Description: The Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS) is sponsored by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. The MHS produces monthly regional estimates of the average sales price for new manufactured homes and more detailed annual estimates including selected characteristics of new manufactured homes. In addition, MHS produces monthly estimates of homes shipped by status. The statistics on shipments of new manufactured homes are produced by the Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS). They are rounded in the month of release and unrounded in subsequent months. Both not seasonally adjusted and seasonally adjusted annual rates of shipment estimates of new manufactured homes are released monthly.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS): Research Report

**Your description is accurate.** It matches, nearly word for word, the official "About" text on both the Census Bureau's MHS page and HUD USER's MHS page. A few points it leaves out are worth adding:

- The official text adds that seasonally adjusted shipments for the current year and the previous five years are revised each year when April shipments are released.
- Coverage is limited to new homes that received a federal inspection ("HUD-code" homes).
- Shipment counts are not survey estimates. IBTS produces them, and they also serve as the list the Census Bureau samples from and the totals it adjusts its estimates to.
- The name is used inconsistently. Some Census systems, including the API, call it the "Manufactured **Homes** Survey."

---

## 1. Who publishes it

| Role | Entity |
|---|---|
| Sponsor and funder | U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R) |
| Data collection, processing and publication | U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce), Economic Indicators / Construction programs |
| Shipment counts and sampling list | Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS), HUD's contracted monitoring agent for the federal Manufactured Housing Program |
| Secondary distribution | HUD USER (huduser.gov) points to Census; FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed) republishes the series |

IBTS says it has managed manufactured home data for HUD for nearly 50 years. It started in the 1970s, when it was organized as the National Conference of States on Building Codes and Standards (NCSBCS), after HUD issued its federal construction standards (the "HUD Code") in 1976. IBTS also holds HUD certification label and data-plate records, so it can issue label verification letters to homeowners.

## 2. Legal authority

**Authorizing statutes.** Census's respondent page cites:
- **42 U.S.C. 5424 note**, from the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980
- **13 U.S.C. § 8(b)**, which lets the Census Bureau do statistical work for other agencies
- **12 U.S.C. § 1701z-1**, HUD's research authority

Together these authorize the survey and make responses **voluntary**.

**Confidentiality.** Under **13 U.S.C. § 9**, responses may be used only for statistical purposes and seen only by sworn Census staff. Copies kept by respondents are immune from legal process. Data are also covered by the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015.

**OMB clearance.**
- Control number **2528-0029** (a HUD number); form **C-MH-9A**.
- The 2021 form showed an expiration date of 7/31/2025.
- HUD published a 60-day notice (89 FR 93648, Nov. 27, 2024) and a 30-day notice (Mar. 6, 2025) asking to **extend** the collection. Estimated burden: 4,860 responses a year, about 20 minutes each, roughly 1,604 hours a year.

**Statutory uses** (from the 2025 Federal Register notice):
- **Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008, § 2145(b)** requires HUD to index FHA Title I manufactured home loan limits every year. MHS single- and double-section prices feed that index.
- A final rule, "Indexing Methodology for Title I Manufactured Home Loan Limits," was published Feb. 28, 2024. Revised limits apply to applications received on or after Mar. 29, 2024.
- The data also let HUD report prices nationally, by region and by state, track whether homes go on owned or rented land, and monitor housing production and affordability.

**Related background.** The National Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974 (42 U.S.C. 5401 et seq.) created the HUD Code, effective June 15, 1976. This is what defines the "HUD-code homes" the survey covers.

## 3. History

- **1959:** The monthly and annual shipment series starts here. (Census doesn't explain where pre-HUD-Code shipment data came from; worth checking if it matters to you.)
- **1974:** Monthly survey begins. Through 1979, dealers in 137 sampling areas reported homes received, placed and held in inventory.
- **1980s:** The program was known as the **"Survey of Mobile Home Placements."** HUD's FY1988 research plan lists it with the American Housing Survey (AHS) and other Census-run housing series. From 1985, the AHS adjusted its mobile home estimates to match this survey's placement counts.
- **After 1979:** A monthly sample of shipped homes. Dealers were phoned every month until the home was placed.
- **1980:** Selected-characteristics data begin.
- **January 2010:** The sample changed from 1-in-40 systematic to a fixed-size sample in each region.
- **August 2014:** Major redesign. Dealers are contacted once, four months after shipment, and asked for an actual or intended sales price. **Data from before 2014 are not comparable** and are kept on a separate "previous series" page.
- **2014:** The annual public-use microdata file (PUF) begins.
- **January 2021:** The form was revised to identify leased units, better separate placed from not-yet-placed homes, and update characteristics questions. The method didn't change, but characteristics data before 2021 come from the old form.
- **2024–25:** OMB extension sought, as noted above.
- **2026:** The program is still active. As of this research (Oct. 2026), recent releases included Sept. 8, 2026 (shipments through July 2026). Annual tables for 2014–2025 were posted in June 2026, along with a 2025 PUF.

## 4. Methodology (for data scientists)

**Population and sample**
- **Target population:** all new HUD-code manufactured home shipments in the U.S.
- **Sampling list:** IBTS's monthly list of HUD-inspected home *sections* shipped. Sections shipped to Canadian dealers or FEMA-only dealers are removed first.
- **Sample:** a systematic sample in each of the four Census regions, about **405 homes a month** (about 4,860 a year). It is drawn fresh each month, so no sample upkeep is needed.
- **FEMA units** are included with certainty for estimation, but their dealers aren't contacted.

**Collection**
- About four months after shipment, a form is mailed to the dealer. Responses come by mail, fax, phone or web, with follow-up calls to non-responders. Collection runs about 11 business days.

**Key items**
- Sales price (actual or intended)
- Status: sold/placed for residential use, intended for residential sale, non-residential use, or other (lost, destroyed, FEMA)
- Characteristics: size, sections, bedrooms, location, titling, leased status, and others

**Missing data**
- Hot-deck imputation fills missing status, destination, lease status, length, width and bedrooms.
- Missing **price is imputed by regression** on square footage and number of sections.

**Weighting**
- Weights are adjusted so estimates match IBTS totals for single- and multi-section homes.

**Seasonal adjustment**
- Shipments are published as seasonally adjusted annual rates (monthly value × 12) and also unadjusted. Rounded in the first release, unrounded later.

**Disclosure protection**
- Cell suppression only (primary and complementary). No noise is added.
- Flags: D = withheld to avoid disclosure; A = relative standard error ≥ 100; Z = fewer than 50 units; NA = not available.

## 5. Data products and access

**Monthly**
- Shipments: SA and NSA, U.S. and regions
- Shipments by status (from Jan. 2014)
- Average sales price by region and size, by month of shipment (from 2014)

**Annual**
- Average price by state
- Average and median square footage by region
- Selected characteristics by region (back to 1980 in older series)
- "Cost & Size Comparison: New Manufactured vs. New Single-Family Site-Built Homes"

**Microdata (PUF), annual from 2014**
- Variables include CONTROL, REGION, SHIPMONTH, SECTIONS, WEIGHT, WGTADJ, price and characteristics.
- Record counts vary with FEMA activity: 2022 had 7,023 records (2,163 of them FEMA units); 2023 had 6,017 (1,158 FEMA); 2025 had 4,859 (0 FEMA).

**Census Data API** (requires a key)
- `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/mhs` for the older series
- `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/mhs2` for 2014 to present

Census lists MHS in its economic indicator time series but says it is **not a principal economic indicator**.

**Other access**
- Census time-series/trend chart tool (program code MHS2)
- PDF tables on www2.census.gov
- FRED series (e.g., SPSNSAUS, SPDNSAUS, SPTNSAUS), with past versions of each release in **ALFRED**

**Recent values (for scale)**
- Seasonally adjusted shipments ran about 96,000–108,000 a year in 2025 and about 95,000–106,000 through July 2026.
- The peak in the current series was about 122,000 (early 2022). The low was 73,000 (April 2020).
- Average price, March 2025: about **$124,500 total**, $83,800 single-section, $153,800 double-section.
- For comparison, the 2019 average was $81,900 for 1,448 sq ft.

## 6. Caveats for analysts

1. **The 2014 break.** Don't join pre- and post-2014 status or price series.
2. **Price includes intended prices** and covers the **home only** (no land, and usually no site work). Prices are indexed to *shipment* month, so price data lag about five months behind shipments.
3. **Small sample.** About 405 homes a month means state, region and month cells can be noisy. Check standard errors and the A and Z flags.
4. **Coverage.** HUD-code homes only. Excludes modular homes, pre-1976 mobile homes, and resales of existing homes. It says nothing about financing (HMDA is the source for that).
5. **FEMA disaster units** can swing shipment counts.
6. **Characteristics questions changed in 2021.**
7. **Revisions.** Seasonally adjusted shipments are revised each April release for six years. Use ALFRED to recover earlier versions.

## 7. Typical users

- **HUD:** FHA Title I loan-limit indexing, Manufactured Housing Program oversight, affordability monitoring
- **FHFA, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac:** "Duty to Serve" plans. FHFA has cited the MHS Cost & Size table (2019: about $60/sq ft for manufactured homes vs. $119/sq ft for site-built).
- **CFPB:** manufactured housing finance reports
- **Census Bureau itself:** historically used to set the AHS mobile home controls
- **Industry:** the Manufactured Housing Institute, manufacturers (e.g., Clayton), lenders, investors and analysts (e.g., Berkadia's annual report), trade press
- **Researchers and nonprofits:** Urban Institute, Pew, Harvard JCHS, the BIS (which cited 2019 MHS prices), Prosperity Now
- **State housing finance agencies, planners, journalists and advocates** working on affordable housing, zoning or resident-owned communities

## 8. Public benefits

- It is the **only official, nationally consistent measure of new manufactured home prices and placements**. Manufactured homes are among the cheapest unsubsidized paths to owning a home: about 6% of owner-occupied units, housing over 17 million people.
- It is built into a **legal formula** (HERA §2145 loan limits), which directly affects how much low- and moderate-income buyers can borrow.
- It provides evidence for **zoning, financing and chattel-vs-real-property titling** debates, since titling and land-tenure data come from the survey.
- It helps track the supply of affordable homes and disaster-related production (FEMA).
- Data and microdata are free, with an API and FRED distribution.

## 9. Preservation and policy risk

- **Dependence on HUD funding.** MHS is paid for from PD&R's Research & Technology account. The FY2026 President's Budget proposed cutting that account by **32% ($44M)**, according to CRS. In 2025 HUD **postponed the AHS** collection, a first since the 1980s, citing cost and a change in method. MHS hasn't been reported as cut, but it relies on the same budget line.
- **Single point of failure.** The sampling list comes from one contractor, IBTS. A contract lapse would affect both the counts and the sample.
- **OMB clearance** has to be renewed regularly. The 2025 extension request is in the record.
- **What to archive:**
  - The Census MHS pages: methodology, the respondent page with its authority text, both questionnaires (2014–2020 and 2021 to present), and the previous-series/historic data pages
  - All annual PUFs and their documentation
  - Monthly PDF tables
  - API snapshots of the mhs and mhs2 endpoints
  - ALFRED release versions
  - HUD Federal Register notices (89 FR 93648; the Mar. 6, 2025 notice) and the Feb. 28, 2024 Title I indexing rule
  - HUD USER's mirror page

  Note that FederalRegister.gov blocks automated scraping, so use its API.
- **Contacts and points of reference:** Census Economic Indicators Division (construction statistics); HUD PD&R; OMB 2528-0029 on reginfo.gov.

**Not verified:** the source of the 1959–1973 shipment data; the exact 2025 annual average price (I saw only monthly figures and secondary estimates of about $123–127K); and whether the 2025 OMB extension has been approved and what its new expiration date is. Check reginfo.gov for OMB 2528-0029 to confirm the current status.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

Next I'll check whether the MHS schedule itself slipped and has since recovered.# Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS): Risk Assessment
*As of Oct. 9, 2026*

**Overall:** the MHS is still running and publishing on schedule, and its OMB clearance is current. The main risk comes from staff losses and funding pressure at HUD and the Census Bureau, the two agencies it depends on. Nothing I found targets the MHS directly. The one real disruption since January 2025 was the fall 2025 government shutdown, which delayed two monthly releases.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence of risk:**
- None found. I found no sign of removed files, deleted variables or warnings on the site.

**Evidence of no issue:**
- The Census "Latest Data" page was updated Oct. 6, 2026. It still offers monthly shipments for 1959–2020 and 2021–2026, monthly shipments to states (2000–2026), and annual state totals (1994–2026). ([Census Latest Data](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/mhs/data/latest-data.html))
- Average-price and home-status tables go back to 2014. The pre-2014 series is still on its separate "previous data" page.
- Public-use microdata files are posted for every year from 2014 through 2025.
- Outside copies exist. ALFRED keeps every MHS release since June 2020 (28 series), and FRED republishes the main series. ([ALFRED release 471](https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/release?rid=471))
- Breaks in the series (2014 redesign, 2021 form change) are documented methodology changes, not removals.

**Rating:** No Known Issue. All earlier data are still available with no known changes.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk** (borderline No Known Issue)

**Evidence for Moderate:**
- The scheduled Oct. 6 and Nov. 6, 2025 releases did not happen. ALFRED shows no MHS releases between Sept. 8 and Dec. 4, 2025, even though Census had scheduled both. ([2025 release schedule](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/programs-surveys/mhs/2025-releasedates.pdf))
- The cause was the funding lapse from Oct. 1 to Nov. 12, 2025. Census said no collection or processing could happen for the October reference month. ([Census recovery plan](https://www.census.gov/econ/indicators/census-pfei-recovery-2025-lapse-in-funding.pdf))

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- **The OMB clearance is current.** The clearance (OMB 2528-0029) was due to expire July 31, 2025. OMB approved the extension without change on **Apr. 15, 2025**, before it lapsed. ([reginfo history](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAOMBHistory?ombControlNumber=2528-0029)) I didn't confirm the new expiration date; it would normally be about April 2028.
- Every release since Dec. 4, 2025 has come out as scheduled, including Oct. 6, 2026. The Oct. 2026 release covers August 2026 shipments and May 2026 prices, the usual lag, so there is no remaining backlog. ([FRED 2026 calendar](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/releases/calendar?rid=471&y=2026))
- The annual tables for 2014–2025 and the 2025 microdata file came out in June 2026 as usual.

**Rating:** Moderate. Two scheduled releases were missed during the assessment period, which matches the rubric's "publication date missed / delayed." The cause was government-wide and has been fully fixed, so this could also be rated No Known Issue.

---

## 3. Data Quality: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence of risk:**
- The shutdown created a two-month publication gap. Census's recovery plan for its main economic indicators involved shorter response windows and less review time. MHS isn't one of those main indicators, so it's unclear whether those shortcuts applied to it.
- Staff losses at Census (about 1,300–1,500 people) and HUD (about 3,000) put pressure on the people who review and run the survey. See section 5.
- The survey is small (about 405 homes a month), so a drop in response rates or review quality would quickly make the estimates noisier.

**Evidence of no issue:**
- Detail is unchanged: regions, state averages, home size, status and characteristics.
- Monthly and annual frequency is maintained, and the usual release lag has returned.
- The 2025 approval kept the same 4,860 responses a year and the same form (C-MH-9A). Nothing was cut.

**Rating:** Moderate. There has been no actual loss of detail, timeliness or frequency, but there are signs of strain.

---

## 4. Statutory Context: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence of risk:**
- The basic authority is discretionary. The Housing and Community Development Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 5424 note) gives the HUD Secretary discretion to take necessary actions. It doesn't order a specific survey or schedule.
- Collection is voluntary under Title 13.
- No statute names "the MHS" as such.

**Evidence of no issue:**
- **A federal program depends on it.** HERA 2008 §2145(b) requires HUD to adjust FHA Title I manufactured home loan limits every year. HUD's Feb. 28, 2024 final rule uses MHS single- and double-section prices for that index, and HUD repeated this in its 2025 renewal notice. ([90 FR 11431](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-03-06/html/2025-03597.htm))
- **There is no substitute source.** IBTS provides shipment counts only, with no prices, placements or characteristics. The ACS and AHS cover existing housing, not new HUD-code sales prices. Private data cover only part of the market.
- The authorities are spelled out: 42 U.S.C. 5424 note, 13 U.S.C. 8(b), and 12 U.S.C. 1701z-1.

**Rating:** No Known Issue. A federal program needs the data and nothing else can replace them. The one weakness is that HUD could, in principle, rewrite its indexing rule to use another source.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**

**Evidence for High:**
- **HUD** has about 5,800 employees, down from about 8,800 in FY2024. That is roughly 3,000 people, or about 34%, mostly through the 2025 deferred resignation program. HUD's own withdrawn draft said some offices were "particularly impacted." ([Federal News Network, Sept. 2026](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/reorganization/2026/09/hud-circulated-plans-for-a-major-reorganization-then-it-withdrew-them/))
- **Census Bureau** lost about 1,300–1,500 workers to deferred resignation and early retirement in 2025. About 100 more got layoff notices during the shutdown. ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/census-bureau-doge-federal-surveys-fe560e377be69e913660a6d90c1ee419); [Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/census-bureau-hit-with-layoffs-as-100-get-notices-in-shutdown))
- **Leadership:** Census Director Robert Santos resigned in 2025, and the Bureau has since been run by an acting leader with no Senate-confirmed director. AP reported 18 vacancies on the top-leadership roster.
- Both agencies' losses exceed the rubric's 1,000-staff threshold.

**Evidence that softens this:**
- **Funding.** The FY2026 budget proposed cutting HUD's Research & Technology account, which pays for the MHS, by 32% (from $139M to $95M). ([HUD FY26 budget justification](https://www.hud.gov/sites/dfiles/CFO/documents/2026_CJ_Program_PDR.pdf)) Congress rejected most of that in the appropriations law signed Feb. 3, 2026 (P.L. 119-75). CRS's table appears to show about **$123M** for the account, roughly 11% below FY2025, but I couldn't fully confirm that figure. The FY2025 total also included $20M for eviction-protection grants, so research and survey money may actually be close to flat. ([CRS R48728](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48728))
- Congress set PD&R's salaries line at $31.5M. ([FY26 joint explanatory statement](https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/fy26_thud_jes.pdf))
- The administration's own budget still lists the MHS as one of the surveys it would fund.
- The usajobs tracker you suggested had no data I could use: it stopped updating Dec. 31, 2025 and its figures load dynamically. The staffing numbers above come from news coverage instead.

**Rating:** High. Both agencies fall under the rubric's high-risk triggers (≥1,000 staff lost, and the Census director's departure). I found no evidence that MHS staff in particular were cut.

---

## 6. Policy: **No Known Issue** (with indirect pressures)

**Evidence of risk:**
- The FY2026 budget proposed a 32% cut to the account that funds the MHS (section 5).
- In 2025 HUD postponed the American Housing Survey, its sister survey, for the first time since the 1980s, citing cost and a move to continuous collection. This shows PD&R-funded Census surveys can be delayed. ([Streetlight](https://streetlightnews.org/american-housing-survey/))
- HUD drafted a reorganization in 2026 that would have consolidated PD&R, then withdrew it. ([Federal News Network](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/reorganization/2026/09/hud-circulated-plans-for-a-major-reorganization-then-it-withdrew-them/))
- The AHS's 2025 approval came with an "E.O. 14168" condition (the executive order on gender ideology). This doesn't affect the MHS, which collects no information about people.

**Evidence of no issue:**
- The MHS renewal was approved "without change" in April 2025, with the same scope.
- I found no presidential action or warning note on the site, and no announced changes to what the MHS collects or publishes.
- The administration's FY2026 budget names the MHS as a survey it plans to continue.

**Rating:** No Known Issue. Nothing since January 2025 has changed what the MHS collects or publishes. The pressures above are indirect, but worth watching, especially as an AHS-style postponement would be a sign of trouble.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

- **Historical Data Availability:** No Known Issue
- **Future Data Availability:** Moderate Risk
- **Data Quality:** Moderate Risk
- **Statutory Context:** No Known Issue
- **Staffing and Funding:** High Risk
- **Policy:** No Known Issue

**Preservation advice:** the risk is low to moderate overall. The most useful steps:
- Save copies of the annual microdata files and the "previous series" pages.
- Rely on ALFRED for earlier versions of each release.
- Watch the next OMB renewal (around 2028).
- Watch HUD's FY2027 budget request for the research account.
